VeriLLM: A Lightweight Framework for Publicly Verifiable Decentralized Inference

Ke Wang Affiliation: Gradient Network
Email: wangke@gradient.network    Felix Qu Affiliation: National University of Singapore

Abstract

Decentralized inference is an appealing paradigm for serving large language models (LLMs), offering strong security, high efficiency, and lower operating costs. Yet the permissionless setting admits no a priori trust in participating nodes, making output verifiability a prerequisite for secure deployment.

We present VeriLLM, a publicly verifiable protocol for decentralized LLM inference that (i) achieves security under a one-honest-verifier assumption, (ii) attains near-negligible verification cost (≈1\approx 1% of the underlying inference) via a lightweight verification algorithm designed explicitly for LLMs, and (iii) enforces honest checking through a peer-prediction mechanism that mitigates lazy verification in naive voting. We further introduce an isomorphic inference–verification network that multiplexes both roles on the same set of GPU workers. This architecture (i) increases GPU utilization and thereby improves end-to-end throughput for both inference and verification, (ii) expands the effective pool of available validators, strengthening robustness and security, and (iii) enforces task indistinguishability at the worker boundary to prevent job-type–conditioned behavior.

Finally, we provide a formal game-theoretic analysis and prove that, under our incentives, honest inference and verification constitute a Nash equilibrium, ensuring incentive compatibility against rational adversaries. To our knowledge, this is the first decentralized inference verification protocol with an end-to-end game-theoretic security proof.

I Introduction

The rapid rise of Large Language Models (LLMs) stems from their strong utility in various areas, including writing code and creative tasks, leading to rapid adoption in both business and research. However, this success also highlights a key problem with current AI infrastructure: the massive models and computing power needed to run them are concentrated within a few large technology companies. This concentration of core resources creates broad risks, including privacy loss, limited access, single points of failure, and monopolistic control.

In response to these challenges, the paradigm of decentralized inference [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] offers a promising alternative. By distributing control over data, computational resources, and algorithms across a diverse network of participants, this model inherently promotes greater transparency, fairness, and systemic resilience. It fosters a more competitive innovation landscape by broadening access to foundational AI resources, thereby reducing dependency on centralized gatekeepers and mitigating the risks associated with their concentrated power.

However, a core challenge in this decentralized paradigm is verifiability. In a permissionless network without inherent trust, the system must ensure the correctness of outputs despite potentially faulty or adversarial providers. Without robust verification, participants could respond with arbitrary or incorrect results, severely degrading system reliability. The risk extends beyond mere malfeasance; it includes providers who, in pursuit of cost and efficiency, make opaque optimizations that alter the computational integrity of the model. Common practices—such as using lower numerical precision, compressing the KV-Cache, altering model weights through pruning or distillation, or even modifying input prompts for commercial alignment—can fundamentally change the output in subtle but critical ways [8]. These undisclosed modifications create significant downstream risks for applications that depend on the deterministic quality of LLM outputs, making independent verification not just a security feature but a prerequisite for trustworthy inference.

Existing approaches to verification—mainly cryptographic proofs and consensus-based replication—face significant practical limitations. Zero-knowledge proof systems can, in principle, attest to the correctness of neural network inference, but current general-purpose and ML-tailored proof systems impose overheads that exceed native inference cost by orders of magnitude for LLMs, especially at realistic sequence lengths and model sizes [9, 10, 11, 12]. This renders them economically infeasible for high-throughput serving today. Consensus-style schemes replicate inference across multiple nodes and accept majority or supermajority agreement, or employ interactive verification games; these rely on brittle assumptions (e.g., an honest majority, independence of failures, or strong synchrony) and incur substantial excess computation and latency [13, 14, 15]. Moreover, both families are poorly compatible with modern blockchain environments when public verifiability is required: on-chain verification of large ML proofs remains expensive, deterministic numeric reproducibility across heterogeneous hardware is challenging, and data-availability constraints complicate transparent auditing.

To address these challenges, we present VeriLLM, a novel publicly verifiable protocol for decentralized LLM inference that simultaneously addresses the trilemma of trust assumptions, computational cost, and verification reliability. Our solution provides: (i) security under a one-honest-verifier assumption, eliminating the need for honest-majority models; (ii) near-negligible verification cost (approximately 1% of the underlying inference); and (iii) collusion-resistant verification through a peer-prediction mechanism that prevents lazy validation.

To achieve security under a one-honest-verifier assumption while keeping costs low, we adopt a hybrid design that combines lightweight empirical rerunning with cryptographic verification-based decisions. First, all intermediate hidden states are committed to Merkle trees with on-chain root hashes, yielding tamper-evident logs and binding evidence for later checks; Second, a verifiable random function (VRF) selects unpredictable verification positions, at which any verifier can empirically rerun the corresponding computations off-chain and compare against the committed values; and Third, a dispute-resolution protocol allows any honest verifier to challenge mismatches by submitting Merkle proofs of inconsistency, with escalation to zero-knowledge proofs when necessary for definitive adjudication. This hybrid approach keeps typical verification overhead low via sampled reruns, yet guarantees that a single honest verifier can detect and prove misconduct with overwhelming probability.

To achieve minimal verification cost, we exploit the computational structure of LLM inference. A typical pipeline consists of a Prefill phase followed by a sequential, autoregressive Decoder phase, with the latter constituting the primary computational bottleneck [16]. We observe that when the complete output sequence is known to verifiers, the expensive Decoder phase can be bypassed: verifiers need only execute the Prefill computation to validate the inference. This approach reduces the verification overhead to a small fraction of the full inference cost.

To achieve public verifiability and prevent lazy verification, we implement a blockchain-based protocol with an incentive-compatible token economy that preserves system liveness. First, we adopt a two-layer verification mechanism that minimizes on-chain costs: computationally intensive checks are executed off-chain by selected verifiers, while the blockchain performs lightweight spot checks and adjudicates disputes. Second, we derive randomness from on-chain commitments to sample positions in the final-token hidden state; for each sample, verifiers submit lightweight on-chain checks (e.g., Merkle openings with minimal recomputation) that attest they actually executed the required computations. A peer-prediction mechanism discourages collusion by rewarding reports that align with the distribution expected from an honest majority.

Building upon this foundation, we replace the traditional heterogeneous Inferencer–Verifier architecture with an isomorphic network in which all GPU workers multiplex both roles. The system no longer distinguishes Inferencer nodes from Verifier nodes, and workers do not distinguish verification tasks from inference tasks; in fact, a worker cannot tell which type of job it is executing. This task indistinguishability at the worker boundary improves security by preventing job-type–conditioned behavior.

Finally, we provide a formal game-theoretic analysis proving that honest inference and verification constitute a Nash equilibrium under our incentive structure, ensuring incentive compatibility against rational adversaries. To our knowledge, this represents the first decentralized inference verification protocol with an end-to-end, game-theoretic security proof, providing strong theoretical foundations for practical deployment in adversarial environments.

We summarize our contributions as follows:

  • •

    Single-Honest-Verifier Security: We establish a novel security model that requires only one honest verifier, achieved through Merkle commitments, VRF-based sampling, and an escalatory dispute resolution protocol.

  • •

    Minimal Verification Cost: We formalize a verification approach requiring only the Prefill phase computation, reducing verification cost to approximately 1% of full inference.

  • •

    Public Verification and Lazy-Verification Prevention: We introduce an on-chain sampling mechanism with two-layer verification and peer-prediction incentives to ensure validators actually perform computations.

  • •

    Isomorphic inference–verification network: We propose an isomorphic inference–verification network that co-schedules indistinguishable inference and verification jobs on the same GPU workers.

  • •

    Security Analysis and Game-Theoretic Foundations: We provide a comprehensive security analysis against practical attacks (quantization, early-stop, forged-output) and establish the first formal game-theoretic proof that honest participation constitutes a Nash equilibrium under our incentive mechanisms.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 discusses related work in decentralized inference and verification mechanisms. Section 3 introduces our background and problem statement. Section 4 details the core protocol design, including the commit-sample-verify pipeline and incentive mechanisms. Section 5 provides formal security and game-theoretic analysis. Section 6 presents experimental results and performance evaluation. Finally, Section 7 concludes with directions for future work.

II Related Work

II-A Activation Sampling & Compact Commitment

Lightweight methods verify inference integrity by selectively committing to critical activation states. TOPLOC/INTELLECT [8] commits to the top-128 final-layer activations every 32 tokens, compressing data 1000× via polynomial congruence (258 bytes per commitment). However, its verification process requires a trusted third party to re-run the computation and provide a ground truth, which reintroduces a central trust assumption. TensorBlock [17] extends this to KV-cache sampling using deterministic token/layer selection, enabling validators to recompute partial trajectories from checkpoints. VeriSplit [18] supports private outsourcing through linear operator masking: clients add noise to inputs, workers return encrypted activations, and clients locally denoise results using precomputed terms, with Merkle trees enabling partial verification. However, their probabilistic security cannot guarantee the detection of sophisticated model tampering, and input privacy relies on noise injection techniques that are vulnerable to advanced reconstruction attacks.

II-B Zero-Knowledge Machine Learning (ZKML)

Sumcheck-based Protocols: zkCNN [19] accelerates convolution verification by transforming operations to the frequency domain. zkLLM [11] reduces communication by 90% for non-arithmetic operations (e.g., Softmax) via the tlookup protocol and exploits translation invariance. QAP-based Protocols: vCNN [20] represents convolutions as Quadratic Polynomial Programs (QPP), reducing multiplicative gates exponentially. pvCNN [21] further optimizes tensor operations via Quadratic Matrix Programs (QMP) and batch verification. ZKML [10] offers modular circuit design with 43 pre-built layer circuits and automated optimization. zkGPT [12] leverages multi-thread parallelization for LLM inference-proof acceleration. Lookup arguments [22] enable matrix-level privacy with 30% faster proofs. VOLE-based Protocols: Mystique [23] achieves sublinear communication for matrix multiplication using sVOLE-based tensor compression. Recent frameworks [24] optimize nonlinear functions via table lookups and digital decomposition, reducing constraints by over 99%.

System & Hardware Optimization: zkLoRA [25] supports verifiable fine-tuning via incremental proofs for LoRA modules. EZKL [9] automates ZKP circuit generation from ONNX models. DeepProve [26] accelerates GPU-based ZKML (54–158× faster proofs via parallelized SNARKs). Sertn [27] employs optimistic ”Staked Deferred Proofs” with economic slashing for invalid results. However, these methods impose prohibitive prover costs (hours per inference), require trusted setups, and suffer from rigidity in supporting novel architectures due to circuit specialization.

However, these works come with severe drawbacks, including prohibitive prover costs (often hours per inference), the need for trusted setups in many schemes, and architectural rigidity that hinders support for novel operators due to specialized circuit designs.

II-C Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs)

Atoma Network [28] combines TEE attestation with sampling-based consensus for deterministic execution. evML [29] uses TEE-based remote attestation (e.g., Google/Apple frameworks) with probabilistic auditing. nesa.ai [30] orchestrates heterogeneous TEEs for secure multi-party inference. Phala Network [31] extends this paradigm by providing a ”Confidential AI” cloud platform that enables standard Dockerized AI applications to run within GPU-equipped TEEs. However, they inherit vulnerabilities to side-channel exploits (e.g., cache-timing attacks), centralize trust in proprietary hardware (Intel SGX/ARM TrustZone), and exhibit limited auditability across heterogeneous environments.

II-D Consensus & Optimistic Approaches

Verde [13] employs optimistic dispute resolution, recomputing only divergent operators (e.g., single attention heads) to minimize overhead. Mira [14] leverages multi-model consensus against hallucinations using domain-specific thresholds. Ambient [15] introduces Proof-of-Logits (PoL), hashing intermediate logits for spot-check verification at <0.1%<0.1\% overhead. However, they introduce delayed finality during dispute windows and implicitly assume honest majority participation.

III Background & Problem Statements

Full-Sequence Prefill for Parallel Verification. In autoregressive LLMs, causal (left-to-right) attention enforces that the hidden state at position tt depends on all preceding tokens, which in turn forces decoding to proceed strictly token by token and limits parallelism. Because the prompt is known a priori, practical systems first run a prefill phase: they compute, in parallel, the representations for all prompt tokens and materialize the key–value (KV) cache, thereby accelerating the subsequent step-wise decode. The same idea applies even more strongly at verification time. Given that the verifier observes the entire sequence (prompt concatenated with the produced output), it can perform a single full-sequence prefill under the causal mask to obtain all token representations in one pass, eliminating the expensive autoregressive decoding loop. Empirically, this reduces the verifier’s computation to roughly ∼1%\sim 1\% of the original generation time, rendering the verification overhead effectively negligible.

Lazy Verification. A naïve validation strategy is to have each Verifier re-execute the forward pass under the same model and hyperparameters as the Inferencer and compare the resulting intermediate states against those declared by the Inferencer; the system then aggregates verdicts by majority vote. This baseline, however, creates a lazy-verification incentive: because the Inferencer is honest in the vast majority of cases, a rational Verifier may skip computation and simply report True, quietly eroding security. We address this with a lightweight commit–sample–check protocol. Each Verifier posts a binding commitment to its Boolean verdict and hidden states. The contract then draws a set of token indices and requires the Verifier to open the corresponding hidden states on-chain. The contract checks agreement between the openings and the Inferencer’s committed states; a mismatch that contradicts the Verifier’s declared verdict triggers slashing, while consistent openings earn a reward. Because hidden-state computations exhibit floating-point nondeterminism, the resulting comparisons are unavoidably noisy; consequently, the practical protocol is more intricate. In the following section, we present a noise-robust, secure scheme and provide a game-theoretic analysis of incentives under bounded numerical error.

Security under Sampling Majority. Conventional consensus protocols assume a majority of honest participants and prove safety under that premise. In contrast, our verification protocol achieves safety under the strictly weaker one-honest-verifier (OHV) assumption; moreover, we show that when verifiers are majority-honest, safety holds even without zero-knowledge proofs. A key difference from consensus is that inference checks involve a randomly sampled, small committee rather than the full network. Consequently, an adversary controlling only a minority of nodes still has non-zero probability of capturing a given committee and biasing a verdict. We conduct a systematic analysis of this sampling attack and mitigate it through a purpose-designed verifier-selection mechanism together with a reverify scheme.

IV Protocol Design

IV-A System Model

VeriLLM is a publicly verifiable, decentralized inference system for large language models (LLMs) built atop blockchain. The system comprises three components—(i) a scheduler, (ii) homogeneous node groups, and (iii) on-chain verification contracts—coordinated to deliver auditably correct inference with low verification overhead.

  1. 1.

    Scheduler. The scheduler orchestrates inference task placement and the logging/forwarding of intermediate hidden states. For each incoming job, it first selects a set of eligible node groups that can jointly serve the task. Within each selected group, it designates one Inferencer and several Verifiers, with the latter responsible for verifying the former’s outputs. Although logically centralized, the scheduler derives both role assignment and verification checkpoint sampling from a verifiable random function (VRF), ensuring unpredictability and public non-manipulability.

  2. 2.

    Node groups. Nodes are organized into groups of homogeneous or near-homogeneous GPU workers. Owing to GPU memory constraints, each worker may host only a slice of the model. Concretely, every node in a group hosts an identical copy of the same Transformer block (layer)—including all weights, layer-norm statistics, and kernel configurations. For any inference job, a node may be assigned as an Inferencer or as a Verifier, as determined by the scheduler. For each job, a VRF-driven scheduler designates one Inferencer and several Verifiers. The execution interface and inputs are deliberately role-agnostic. At the onset of Prefill, a worker typically cannot tell whether its computation serves the live inference pipeline or a verification probe. This task-type indistinguishability reduces the opportunity for strategic misbehavior by would-be Verifiers.

  3. 3.

    Verification contracts. A set of on-chain smart contracts that (i) collect verifier-submitted results, (ii) validate these results and finalize them via contract-level consensus, and (iii) dispense incentives accordingly. Participation requires that all roles stake tokens in the contracts, which may be slashed upon adverse outcomes.

End-to-end workflow. (1) A client submits an inference request to the scheduler, which first selects the node groups that can jointly serve the job and then, using a VRF, chooses one Inferencer and several Verifiers from each group. (2) The Inferencer executes the forward pass in a pipelined manner, streaming intermediate hidden states to the scheduler; the scheduler records these hidden states and forwards them among inference nodes as needed. (3) After inference completes, the scheduler dispatches the corresponding initial hidden states to the assigned Verifiers. Each Verifier runs a prefill computation to reproduce the target hidden states, compares them with the Inferencer’s hidden states, and submits the comparison result to the smart contract on-chain. (4) To deter “lazy” verification, the scheduler samples hidden-state indices; Verifiers must submit the sampled hidden states for on-chain comparison, and the contract rewards or penalizes Verifiers according to the on-chain outcome.

IV-B Registration

To deter dishonest behavior, both the scheduler and worker nodes must register and lock collateral in on-chain smart contracts. Scheduler registration includes (i) submitting the VRF verification public key so that VRF outputs used for assignment and sampling can be validated, and (ii) publishing a network endpoint to enable node–scheduler communication. Node registration includes (i) declaring the hosted model and the specific layer it serves, and (ii) publishing a reachable endpoint for interaction by the scheduler and peer nodes.

Nodes may deregister to reclaim their stake; withdrawals are subject to a fixed waiting period, allowing the contracts sufficient time to detect and finalize penalties for any misbehavior attributable to the node.

IV-C Schedule Scheme

The Scheduler coordinates node selection and Hidden-State (HS) forwarding for pipeline inference. To minimize latency and simplify flow control, the Scheduler is implemented as a centralized service. To prevent manipulation of node assignments or HS sampling, all scheduling and sampling decisions are derived from a publicly verifiable random beacon instantiated via a verifiable random function (VRF). The Scheduler’s VRF public key is registered on-chain; every scheduling decision is accompanied by a VRF proof that can be audited off-chain or by smart contracts.

Node state maintenance. The Scheduler continuously watches the on-chain registry for node enrollments, exits, and metadata updates. From this event stream, it maintains a local snapshot of the active population and partitions nodes into homogeneous groups based on the exact model slice that each node hosts. A model slice is a contiguous block of layers. Concretely, for model mm and slice ζ\zeta:

Gm,ζ={n∈𝒩|model(n)=m,slice(n)=ζ}.G_{m,\zeta}\;=\;\{\,n\in\mathcal{N}\;|\;\texttt{model}(n)=m,\ \texttt{slice}(n)=\zeta\,\}.

These groups are the unit of assignment in subsequent scheduling: when serving a request for model m, the Scheduler constructs a pipeline as <Gm,1,Gm,2,⋯,Gm,L><G_{m,1},G_{m,2},\cdots,G_{m,L}> and performs all role selection (inferencer and verifiers) within each group Gm,ζG_{m,\zeta}. Grouping by (m,ζ)(m,\zeta) ensures that every stage operates on nodes with identical functionality, simplifying orchestration and enabling deterministic, reproducible scheduling.

Task Scheduling. Upon receiving a request req, the Scheduler first identifies a chain of node groups that can jointly execute the model (each group hosts the same model segment). Let ii be the pipeline position of group GiG_{i} and Li=∣Gi∣L_{i}=\mid G_{i}\mid its cardinality. To prevent manipulation in role assignment, the Scheduler derives a per-stage, publicly verifiable seed via a VRF bound to the request hash h←H⁡(req)h\leftarrow H(\texttt{req}), the stage index ii, and the group size LiL_{i}. Using the Scheduler’s VRF secret key s​ks​c​hsk_{sch} (with verification key v​ks​c​hvk_{sch} registered on-chain), the seed is:

ri←VRF⁡(s​k𝗌𝖼𝗁,h,i,Li).r_{i}\leftarrow\mathrm{VRF}(sk_{\mathsf{sch}},\,h,\,i,\,L_{i}).

And anyone can check

VRF.Verify⁡(v​k𝗌𝖼𝗁,⟨h,i,Li⟩,ri)≡1.\mathrm{VRF.Verify}(vk_{\mathsf{sch}},\,\langle h,i,L_{i}\rangle,\,r_{i})\equiv 1.

The Scheduler instantiates a permutation σi\sigma_{i} over ∣Li∣\mid L_{i}\mid using a CSPRNG keyed by rir_{i} (e.g., Fisher–Yates with HKDF​(ri)\text{HKDF}(r_{i}). It then deterministically selects one inferencer and kk verifiers within Gm,iG_{m,i}:

niinf=Gm,i[σi(1)],{ni,1ver,…,ni,kver}=Gm,i[σi(2..k+1)].n^{\mathrm{inf}}_{i}\;=\;G_{m,i}[\sigma_{i}(1)],\{n^{\mathrm{ver}}_{i,1},\dots,n^{\mathrm{ver}}_{i,k}\}\;=\;G_{m,i}[\sigma_{i}(2..k{+}1)].

Because the seed binds (h,i,Li)(h,i,L_{i}), any attempt to manipulate node selection is detectable, and the resulting assignments are reproducible and auditable from the on-chain registry and the published VRF proofs.

Hidden-State Forwarding. After node selection, the Scheduler advances pipeline execution by forwarding intermediate hidden states from one inference node to the next, thereby enabling continuous and coordinated computation along the inference pipeline. Concretely, at decoding step tt: (1) the Scheduler delivers the token sequence yty_{t} (for t=1t=1, this is the prompt) to Inferencer i=1; the inferencer locally tokenizes/embeds and runs its hosted layers, producing S2tS_{2}^{t}, which it returns to the Scheduler; (2) the Scheduler forwards S2tS_{2}^{t} to Inferencer i=2i=2 , which computes S3tS_{3}^{t} and returns it; (3) this hop-by-hop relay continues until the tail Inferencer produces the terminal state SL+1tS^{t}_{L+1} and logits and predicts the next token yt+1y_{t+1} and returns to the Scheduler; (4) the Scheduler streams yt+1y_{t+1} to the user and sends the new token back to segment i=1i=1 to start step t+1t+1. The loop halts when yt=<E​O​S>y_{t}=<EOS>.

Hidden-State Logging. To enable post-hoc verification of each inferencer’s computation, the Scheduler records the intermediate hidden states that inferencers submit for every generated token and, after decoding finishes, aggregates these records and delivers them to the corresponding verifiers. To make hidden states tamper-evident, each inferencer deterministically serializes its output tensor SS, builds a Merkle tree over the tensor’s scalar entries, and submits the root γ\gamma with a bound signature Siginf​(h,i,t,γ)\texttt{Sig}_{\text{inf}}(h,i,t,\gamma). To deter forgery in transit, the Scheduler also signs the Hidden States (or its root) it forwards, producing Sigsch​(h,i,t,γ)\texttt{Sig}_{\text{sch}}(h,i,t,\gamma); any mismatch between what was produced and what was relayed is thus attributable. This dual-signature, Merkle-committed transcript makes misrouting or substitution by the Scheduler attributable, tampering by an inferencer detectable, and auditing efficient via selective disclosure of only the needed leaves and paths, without inflating the on-path computation or network cost.

IV-D Inference Scheme

In the inference scheme, we run online, autoregressive generation over a decentralized, pipelined fabric of homogeneous node groups. Each group hosts an identical copy of a contiguous Transformer layer block (including weights, layer‑norm statistics, and kernel configurations). For each task, the Scheduler selects eligible groups and, using a verifiable random function (VRF), assigns one Inferencer per group to execute the live forward pass; verifier roles are drawn by the same VRF but remain inactive during this phase. Throughout generation, the Scheduler relays and logs hidden states across segment boundaries and attaches tamper‑evident commitments and signatures, producing an auditable trace for the subsequent verification phase.

Formally, let the model be partitioned into LL contiguous segments. At token step tt, with causal inputs x1:t=[prompt∥y1:t−1]x_{1:t}=[\texttt{prompt}\,\|\,y_{1:t-1}], the per-segment forward obeys

S1(t)\displaystyle S^{(t)}_{1} ←Embed​(x​1:t),\displaystyle\leftarrow\texttt{Embed}(x{1:t}),
Si+1(t)\displaystyle S^{(t)}_{i+1} ←Fi(Si(t);Wi)(i=1,…,L),\displaystyle\leftarrow F_{i}\big(S^{(t)}_{i};W_{i}\big)\quad(i=1,\dots,L),
yt\displaystyle y_{t} ←Decode​(SL+1(t)).\displaystyle\leftarrow\texttt{Decode}\big(S^{(t)}_{L+1}\big).

where Si(t)S^{(t)}_{i} is the hidden state at the input of segment ii, FiF_{i} is the segment’s forward mapping, WiW_{i} are its parameters, and Decode is the output head coupled with a sampling rule. The end-to-end execution is a token-serial, segment-parallel pipeline synchronized by the Scheduler’s relay of hidden states.

Scheduler-Driven Role Assignment. For each task, the Scheduler enumerates node groups capable of jointly serving the model. Using a VRF, it assigns one Inferencer publicly and non-manipulatively per group. The VRF seeds and proofs are revealed in a manner that makes the selection auditable yet unpredictable ahead of time.

Pipelined Forward and State Relay. During token tt, segment ii’s Inferencer receives from the Scheduler the upstream hidden state Si(t)S^{(t)}_{i} together with a tamper-evidence package: a commitment to the upstream state and a proof of a valid signature from a registered node (or the signature itself, depending on the privacy mode). The Inferencer: (i) performs the forward pass to produce Si+1(t)S^{(t)}_{i+1}; (ii) forms a commitment to Si+1(t)S^{(t)}_{i+1} (e.g., a Merkle root over a canonical serialization) and signs the root with its node key; and (iii) returns {Si+1(t),rooti(t),σi(t)}\{S^{(t)}_{i+1},\texttt{root}^{(t)}_{i},\sigma^{(t)}_{i}\} to the Scheduler. The Scheduler verifies the signature against the on-chain registry (optionally via a zero-knowledge membership proof to hide the signer’s identity), appends its own relay signature, persists the state (disk-backed to reduce memory pressure), and forwards the package to segment i+1i{+}1’s Inferencer. To minimize latency, the receiving Inferencer may begin computing immediately and complete signature/proof verification asynchronously; if verification later fails, the Scheduler aborts and discards all dependent intermediate results.

Commitment and Signature Discipline. For every token and segment boundary, the produced hidden state is anchored by: (i) a commitment rooti(t)=MerkleRoot​(Si+1(t))\texttt{root}^{(t)}_{i}=\texttt{MerkleRoot}(S^{(t)}_{i+1}); and (ii) a node signature σi(t)=Sig​(ski,rooti(t))\sigma^{(t)}_{i}=\texttt{Sig}(\texttt{sk}_{i},\texttt{root}^{(t)}_{i}). Node public keys are registered on-chain under a Merkle accumulator, enabling compact membership proofs. The Scheduler may, instead of forwarding raw signatures, provide a zero-knowledge proof that it holds a valid signature from some registered key on the advertised root, thereby preventing role deanonymization while preserving verifiability. All relayed artifacts are re-signed by the Scheduler to assure origin authenticity and prevent replay.

Autoregressive Token Emission and Feedback. The last segment (i=Li=L) outputs logits (or the final hidden state) for token tt, from which the output token yty_{t} is determined by the prescribed decoding policy. The Scheduler collects yty_{t} and feeds it back to the first segment to form x1:t+1x_{1:t+1}, advancing the pipeline to the next step. This loop repeats until the model emits an end-of-sequence token ⟨EOS⟩\langle\texttt{EOS}\rangle or a stopping criterion is met.

Task-Type Indistinguishability and Robustness. The data formats and RPC interfaces received by Inferencers in this phase are identical to those used by Verifiers during the verification phase. Consequently, a worker cannot reliably infer whether it participates in live inference or a verification probe at the time of computation, reducing avenues for selective deviation. Together with VRF-driven role assignment and signed/committed state relays, this design yields an auditable, tamper-evident inference trace with minimal on-chain overhead during the online phase.

IV-E Verification Scheme

In autoregressive LLM inference, execution begins with a prefill pass—a parallel forward computation over the prompt to construct the KV cache—followed by a serial decoding phase, where per-token dependencies typically dominate latency. This makes inference memory-bound and leads to underutilization of hardware resources. During verification, however, the complete output sequence y1:Ty_{1:T} is known. We can therefore rewrite the input and intermediate Hidden States as

x=[promot∥y1:T],𝒮=[Spromot∥S1∥…∥ST]x=[\texttt{promot}\|y_{1:T}],\mathcal{S}=[S^{\text{promot}}\|S^{1}\|\dots\|S^{T}]

and, under the same causal mask, the verifier can perform a single parallel forward to directly reconstruct the hidden state at every position t∈[1,T]t\in[1,T]. This replaces the TT incremental decoding steps with a single batched pass, avoiding repeated KV-cache updates and cross-node communication, thereby better utilizing specialized GPU components such as Tensor Cores.

Because the Scheduler records, for every token and each segment boundary, the hidden states required to initialize downstream computation, verifiers attached to different node groups can recompute their hosted segment in isolation prefill restricted to their contiguous layer block without consuming any outputs from other verifiers. Thus, verification runs fully in parallel across the LL groups that jointly host the model, and the wall-clock time is dominated by the slowest segment’s prefill. Under near-balanced partitioning and negligible orchestration/I/O overhead, this yields near-linear scaling, giving Tverify≈(1/L)​Tprefill​(full model)T_{\text{verify}}\approx(1/L)T_{\text{prefill}}(\text{full model}).

Prefill Computation. After generation completes, the Scheduler prepares for segment-local verification by delivering to each verifier the start-of-segment hidden states for all tokens—i.e., for segment i>1i>1 it sends the sequence {Si(t)}t=1T\{S_{i}^{(t)}\}_{t=1}^{T} that was produced by the upstream inferencer at the same token steps. (for the first segment it instead supplies the prompt concatenated with the full output token sequence [promot∥y1:T][\texttt{promot}\|y_{1:T}].) Upon receipt, the verifier executes a full sequence prefill limited to its hosted contiguous layer block, using the provided hidden states (or tokens for segment 1) to recompute the segment’s outputs {Si+1(t)}t=1T\{S_{i+1}^{(t)}\}_{t=1}^{T}. Because the Scheduler sends verifiers exactly the same data format and API messages as it sends to inferencers during online inference, a verifier cannot distinguish whether it is serving inference or verification. Consequently, upon completing its computation, the verifier must return the resulting hidden states over the same interface—just as an inferencer would during inference. This indistinguishability removes mode-specific signaling and opportunities for selective deviation, thereby driving verifiers to compute honestly.

Commitment Submission. After completing the prefill recomputation, the Scheduler explicitly advances the verifier to the commit phase. Upon receiving this signal, the verifier forms a tamper-evident commitment to the hidden state of the last generated token (i.e., its segment’s output at step TT). For efficiency, the commitment is instantiated as the Merkle root of a tree built over a canonical serialization of that hidden-state tensor (with scalar entries as leaves). The verifier then publishes the commitment on-chain via the designated contract. This on-chain record provides an immutable anchor for the subsequent verification steps: later, some necessary slices of the hidden state need to be disclosed, accompanied by Merkle inclusion proofs that can be checked against the posted root.

Comparison and On-Chain Commitment. Once all designated verifiers have posted commitments or the commitment deadline elapses, the scheduler disseminates, off-chain, the inferencer-produced target hidden states {Si(t)}t=1T\{S_{i}^{(t)}\}_{t=1}^{T} for all tokens to the corresponding verifier set. Each verifier vv independently validates the entire token sequence through a per-token comparison of its locally computed hidden states with received hidden states {Si(t)}t=1T\{S_{i}^{(t)}\}_{t=1}^{T}. Using task-calibrated summary statistics of the discrepancies—e.g., the empirical error distribution and its mean—it determines whether the inferencer’s computation is correct. Upon comparison, the verifier submits a commitment of its verdict b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\} on-chain:

C=Commit​(b,r).C=\text{Commit}(b,r).

The commitment is used to withhold the submission’s content until the reveal phase, precluding copy-cat behavior by nodes that would otherwise condition their actions on the observed result.

Data Sampling. The goal of data sampling is to check a verifier’s prefill computation on chain with minimal cost, thereby deterring lazy verification. After the verifier posts its verdict, the Scheduler uses a VRF to derive an unbiased set of scalar indices 𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i} over that tensor (sampling all tokens).

(ri,πi)\displaystyle(r_{i},\pi_{i}) ←VRF.Eval​(s​ksch,<h,i,{γj}j=1m>)\displaystyle\leftarrow\text{VRF.Eval}(sk_{\text{sch}},<h,i,\{\gamma_{j}\}_{j=1}^{m}>)
𝒯i\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{i} ←Smaple​(ri,n,q)\displaystyle\leftarrow\text{Smaple}(r_{i},n,q)

It then publishes on chain: the VRF randomness and proof (ri,πi)(r_{i},\pi_{i}), the sampled indices 𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i}, the corresponding scalar values 𝐕𝒯iT\mathbf{V}^{T}_{\mathcal{T}_{i}} extracted from the inferencer-produced hidden state, the inferencer’s signature Sigi,infT\texttt{Sig}_{i,\text{inf}}^{T} over its hidden states’ root γi,infT\gamma_{i,\text{inf}}^{T} and the corresponding Merkle inclusion proofs {MPjinf}j∈𝒯i\{\texttt{MP}_{j}^{\text{inf}}\}_{j\in\mathcal{T}_{i}}, that is

<ri,πi,𝒯i,𝐕𝒯iT,γi,infT,Sigi,infT,{MPjinf}j∈𝒯i><r_{i},\pi_{i},\mathcal{T}_{i},\mathbf{V}^{T}_{\mathcal{T}_{i}},\gamma_{i,\text{inf}}^{T},\texttt{Sig}_{i,\text{inf}}^{T},\{\texttt{MP}_{j}^{\text{inf}}\}_{j\in\mathcal{T}_{i}}>

The contract then performs: (1) VRF check:

VRF.Eval​(v​ksch,<h,i,{γj}j=1m>,πi)≡1\text{VRF.Eval}(vk_{\text{sch}},<h,i,\{\gamma_{j}\}_{j=1}^{m}>,\pi_{i})\equiv 1

ensuring 𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i} was sampled correctly (and bound to request hash hh, segment ii, final step and the posted mm commitments {γj}j=1m\{\gamma_{j}\}_{j=1}^{m}); (2) Origin/authenticity checks: verify Sigi,infT\texttt{Sig}^{T}_{i,\text{inf}} with the VRF-selected inferencer’s registered key, and for each j∈𝒯ij\in\mathcal{T}_{i} validate Merkle proof MPjinf\texttt{MP}_{j}^{\text{inf}} to attest that the reference values indeed come from the correct inferencer’s hidden state. In addition, because the Scheduler signs hidden states it forwards during execution, if the values it publishes differ from what it previously relayed to the inferencer or verifier, either party can file an on-chain complaint, attaching the Scheduler’s relay signature. Upon validation, the Scheduler’s stake will be slashed.

Reveal. The verifier reveal its verdict b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\} on chain and submits to the contract the sampled scalar value {vj}j∈𝒯i\{v_{j}\}_{j\in\mathcal{T}_{i}} together with a Merkle inclusion proof {MPjver}j∈𝒯i\{\texttt{MP}_{j}^{\text{ver}}\}_{j\in\mathcal{T}_{i}} under its posted commitment. The contract will aggregate the verdicts and validates the submitted entries by checking proof {MPjver}j∈𝒯i\{\texttt{MP}_{j}^{\text{ver}}\}_{j\in\mathcal{T}_{i}} and comparing with other verifiers’ submissions. For the tail verifiers (i=Li=L), an additional check is required: the predicted output token must match the token reported by the inferencer. This output-equality guard prevents an inferencer from splicing forged output tokens and performing a cheap full-sequence prefill to evade the expensive decoder computation.

On-Chain Adjudication. For each verification task, the contract first finalizes consensus on verdicts {bv}v∈𝐕\{b_{v}\}_{v\in\mathbf{V}} submitted by verifiers. It then compares each verifier’s revealed samples against the scheduler-published values, passing the check iff the numeric discrepancies lie within the task’s statistical tolerance band.

Dispute. We assume only a global lower bound on the number of honest nodes, while each task samples only mm verifiers. When mm is small, an adversary controlling a modest fraction of the network can, with non-negligible probability, capture the sampled committee (i.e., more than m/2m/2 verifiers). To mitigate this, if the initial outcome is False, the inferencer may request a reconsideration with a larger committee m′>mm^{\prime}>m. If the reconsideration returns True, the contract rescinds the inferencer’s penalty and slashes the first-round verifiers that voted negative. If the reconsideration still returns False, the inferencer bears the cost of the additional verifiers.

V Security Analysis

V-A Threat Model and Assumptions

We consider an adversarial environment with potentially malicious Inferencers, Verifiers, and a curious or even Byzantine Scheduler. Smart contracts are assumed correct and executed as specified.

We list the cryptographic assumptions we used as follows:

  • •

    EUF-CMA security of digital signatures used by nodes.

  • •

    Collision resistance of hash functions and binding of Merkle commitments.

  • •

    Unpredictability and unbiasedness of the VRF used for role assignment.

  • •

    Knowledge of the soundness of any zero-knowledge proofs used to attest signature validity or aggregate Merkle proofs.

We list the system assumptions we used as follows:

  • •

    At least one verifier per job is honest and online. This is strictly weaker than an honest majority assumption and is sufficient to guarantee safety via either (i) statistical hidden-state comparisons and/or (ii) ZK dispute in the worst case.

  • •

    Network is eventually synchronous; the contract enforces timeouts and ordering (commit-then-open) to prevent adaptive cheating.

  • •

    Floating-point nondeterminism is bounded and modeled as small, zero-mean noise; thresholds in our tests are chosen so that honest executions pass with overwhelming probability.

V-B Security Goals

Our scheme provides the following properties.

Completeness. If all parties follow the protocol and run the prescribed model, then both the offline (full hidden-state) and the on-chain (sampled) checks accept except with negligible probability due to benign numeric noise.

Soundness. Any materially incorrect inference (wrong model, manipulated states, or premature stop) is detected with high probability by at least one of: (i) the offline full-sequence checks conducted by verifiers, (ii) the on-chain commit-then-sample audit that forces openings of committed values at unpredictable positions, or (iii) the ZK dispute mechanism that allows a single honest verifier to prove an error.

Trace integrity. Every relayed hidden state at each segment boundary is bound to a tamper-evident commitment signed by a registered node key; the Scheduler cannot alter states without forging signatures or producing an invalid ZK membership proof.

Unpredictable sampling. Sampling indices are derived from commitments fixed prior to seed derivation, preventing adaptive selection of states after seeing the challenge.

Task-type indistinguishability. Workers receive the same data formats and APIs in inference and verification, removing mode-specific signaling and reducing selective deviation.

V-C Commit-Then-Sample: Binding and Unpredictability

Let rir_{i} be the Merkle root committed by node/group ii, and let R=𝖧𝖺𝗌𝗁⁡(r1,…,rn)R=\mathsf{Hash}(r_{1},\dots,r_{n}) be the public seed used to derive sampling positions.

Lemma 1 (Binding).

Given a collision-resistant hash and Merkle tree, a prover that has posted rir_{i} cannot later open an inconsistent value at a sampled index with more than negligible probability.

Lemma 2 (Unpredictability).

If RR is computed from (r1,…,rn)(r_{1},\dots,r_{n}) after all roots are posted on-chain, and the hash is modeled as a random oracle, then the distribution of sampled indices is unpredictable to any party at the time of committing the roots.

Together, these lemmas imply that any party posting a root without computing the corresponding hidden states risks being unable to answer the later opening queries, leading to certain detection and slashing.

V-D Analysis of Concrete Attacks

V-D1 Quantization Attack

An Inferencer runs a quantized model (e.g., W8A8) rather than the prescribed full-precision model to reduce compute.

Defenses. (i) Offline, verifiers perform full-sequence recomputation on their segments and subject the hidden states to hypothesis tests that exploit floating-point statistics (e.g., exponent mismatch rate, mantissa deviation thresholds, cosine similarity). Let ToffT_{\mathrm{off}} denote the conjunction of tests: - fraction P of exponent mismatches is below a small bound, - fraction Q of mantissa diffs below 10−510^{-5} exceeds a high bound, - fraction Z of large mantissa deviations over a threshold is small, - mean absolute mantissa difference falls within a tight interval.

Under the benign-noise model, honest runs pass ToffT_{\mathrm{off}} with probability 1−negl⁡(λ)1-\negl(\lambda); in contrast, quantization induces characteristic, heavy-tailed deviations that violate at least one predicate with high probability (empirically near 100% power under standard quantization settings). (ii) On-chain, a light-weight variant TonT_{\mathrm{on}} is applied to the last token’s hidden state with looser thresholds; this primarily enforces verifier liveness and honesty. Any Inferencer attempting to claim “quantized but close enough” must simultaneously satisfy both offline and on-chain tests, which is statistically unlikely absent running the correct model.

Security claim. For suitably chosen thresholds calibrated on benign nondeterminism, the false-accept probability for a quantized model is negligible in the sequence length and hidden dimension, while honest false-reject remains below the target SLO.

V-D2 Early Termination Attack

The Inferencer stops decoding before producing ⟨EOS⟩\langle\mathrm{EOS}\rangle, saving compute.

Defenses. (i) The last-segment verifier checks that decoding from the final hidden state predicts ⟨EOS⟩\langle\mathrm{EOS}\rangle when claimed, and that the reported output tokens y1:Ty_{1:T} are consistent with the segment outputs. Any premature stop yields a mismatch at the tail token(s) with probability 1. (ii) Because intermediate hidden states at segment boundaries are committed and signed per token, the Scheduler’s audit trail enforces per-step consistency; fabricating terminal states without compute would require forging signatures or breaking Merkle binding.

Security claim. Any premature termination leads to an inconsistency in token prediction or an inability to open committed states, thus being detected with overwhelming probability.

V-D3 Forged Output via Small Model

Use a small model to fabricate an output sequence y~\tilde{y} cheaply; then run full sequence prefill on the large model with [prompt∥y~][\texttt{prompt}\,\|\,\tilde{y}] to produce hidden states that will pass hidden-state-only checks.

Defenses. (i) Verifiers compare the tokens decoded from the recomputed last-layer hidden states against the Inferencer’s published tokens. If y~≠y⋆\tilde{y}\neq y^{\star} (the large model’s decode under the specified policy), the decoded token diverges with nontrivial probability per step; over many positions, the chance that all sampled or checked positions match becomes negligible. (ii) The Scheduler additionally verifies that the input to the first segment at step t+1t{+}1 equals [prompt∥y1:t][\texttt{prompt}\,\|\,y_{1:t}] carried forward from prior steps, tying tokens and hidden states into a single, signed, and committed transcript.

Security claim. Unless the fabricated y~\tilde{y} coincidentally matches the prescribed model’s decode on the checked steps (a negligible event over sufficiently many positions or checks), the attack is detected by token-versus-hidden-state consistency checks.

V-D4 Lazy Verifier (Free-Riding)

A verifier skips prefill and returns an acceptance verdict to earn rewards, relying on the assumption that most Inferencers are honest.

Defenses. (i) Commit-then-open: verifiers must first post a Merkle root of the last token’s hidden state, then later open sampled positions with Merkle proofs. Without actual computation, openings will fail except with negligible probability (due to a hash collision or a lucky guess). (ii) Task-type indistinguishability: since the verification workload uses the same interface as inference, a prover cannot reliably detect probes and selectively compute. (iii) Economic design: only verifiers that pass on-chain checks are rewarded; non-openings or failed openings are penalized (slashed). Peer-prediction style aggregation can further deter coordinated guessing by rewarding agreement within the honest cluster and withholding rewards otherwise.

Security claim. Under Merkle binding and unpredictable sampling, a lazy verifier cannot consistently open correct values and is detected/slashed with overwhelming probability.

V-E Collusion, Censorship, and Dispute

Collusion among verifiers. If a coalition attempts to submit mutually consistent but fabricated hidden states, the commit-then-sample mechanism forces consistency with the fixed root, but does not alone guarantee semantic correctness. Our design, therefore, (i) requires cross-checks of decoded tokens against hidden states, and (ii) admits a ZK dispute path: any single honest verifier can submit a succinct proof of inconsistency with the prescribed model on a challenged prefix, which the contract verifies. Rewards are skewed to make raising correct disputes strictly profitable.

Scheduler misbehavior. The Scheduler cannot alter hidden states without forging node signatures or failing ZK membership proofs. Selective exclusion of registered nodes is detectable by recomputing VRF selections once the signatures/VRF proofs are revealed; contracts can slash the Scheduler upon mismatch.

Censorship resistance. Because commitments are posted on-chain and verifiers are selected via VRF, an adversary must DoS or corrupt all verifiers to prevent detection. Our assumption of at least one honest, live verifier per job suffices to guarantee safety.

V-F Completeness and Soundness Summary

Let ℰ\mathcal{E} denote the event that an incorrect inference passes all checks.

  • •

    If the Inferencer deviates by running the wrong model (e.g., quantized) or fabricating outputs, then either (i) offline full-sequence checks fail with probability 1−negl⁡(λ)1-\negl(\lambda), or (ii) on-chain openings fail due to binding/unpredictability, or (iii) a ZK dispute succeeds. Hence Pr⁡[ℰ]≤negl⁡(λ)\Pr[\mathcal{E}]\leq\negl(\lambda).

  • •

    If all parties are honest and numeric noise respects the calibrated thresholds, the offline and on-chain checks accept with probability 1−δ1-\delta, where δ\delta is set by the system SLO (e.g., δ≤10−3\delta\!\leq\!10^{-3}). Thus completeness holds.

V-G Limitations

Our guarantees rely on at least one honest verifier. A fully colluding ecosystem can still pass statistical checks unless a ZK dispute is mounted. Additionally, the statistical detectors are model- and hardware-calibrated; deploying them on radically different numeric stacks may require retuning the thresholds. Finally, while VRF selection mitigates targeted bias, it cannot prevent the Scheduler from selectively omitting eligible nodes; this is detectable and punishable but not inherently prevented by cryptography.

VI Implementation & Evaluation

We empirically measured the divergence of hidden states produced during inference across heterogeneous compute devices (currently tested on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; additional models are forthcoming). Although floating-point non-determinism across GPU vendors and SKUs introduces small numeric drift, these deviations are limited in magnitude and statistically distinguishable, and consequently, the hidden-state comparison test can, with high probability, determine whether two traces originate from the same underlying model computation.

We further evaluated replacing full-precision models with quantized variants. Hidden states computed by quantized models exhibit substantially larger—and statistically significant—bias relative to the full-precision baseline. Hence, simple statistical tests cleanly separate hidden states from normal inference versus those produced under precision degradation or cheating.

Bit-aware statistical comparison. Let each floating-point value be decomposed into sign, exponent, and mantissa. With tolerances ew>0e_{w}>0 (e.g., ew=10−2e_{w}=10^{-2} and em∈ℕe_{m}\in\mathbb{N} (e.g., em=7e_{m}=7 mantissa steps), we compute:

Guided by our empirical analysis, we adopt task-dependent acceptance thresholds for the statistics (Pe,Pm,Pw,e)(P_{e},P_{m},P_{w},e) defined above. Because off-chain verification compares full hidden states over all tokens, the aggregate statistical error is smaller and tighter tolerances are appropriate; conversely, on-chain verification samples only the final token, which exhibits larger variance and thus warrants looser tolerances. We therefore declare a comparison successful under the following rules:

These thresholds reflect the observed error profiles of the two settings and provide a consistent criterion for determining match/no-match across tasks.

Notably, the on-chain comparison is executed by the contract and therefore uses a unified acceptance standard (the thresholds specified above). By contrast, off-chain comparison is performed by verifiers, who submit only a binary verdict bv∈{0,1}b_{v}\in\{0,1\}; we neither prescribe nor can we audit their internal decision rules. Verifiers are free to adopt custom criteria. However, because rewards are granted only when a verifier’s submission is consistent with the consensus outcome, rational verifiers are incentivized to apply honest and effective comparison methods so that their reported verdicts align with the final decision.

VII Conclusion and Future Work

In this paper, we propose VeriLLM, a protocol for verifiable decentralized LLM inference. It achieves efficient and secure verification under a one-honest-verifier assumption and utilizes game-theoretic incentives to ensure that honest participation is a Nash equilibrium. For future work, we will explore ZK-proofs for stronger collusion resistance, automated threshold calibration for new hardware, and cryptographic mitigations against scheduler censorship.

A Game-Theoretic Proof

-A Modeling and Assumption

We assume that the system randomly draws nn verifiers from a population VV, possibly weighted by stakes. Among the population, each verifier has an independent probability 1−r1-r to be adversarial, and probability rr to be honest. Honest verifiers always verify and report honestly, and adversarial verifiers can behave arbitrarily, possibly colluding with each other.

The protocol requires the nn verifiers to run the same inference task TT for verification, and honest verification incurs a computational cost of cc. The inference result lies in a metric space Ω\Omega with a distance function d:Ω2→[0,+∞)d:\Omega^{2}\to[0,+\infty) that satisfies symmetry and triangle inequality. While the task has an hidden ground-truth result x=x⁡(T)x=x(T), the inference process has a computational noise so that the inference result of each verifier has a small random noise.

We assume that there exists a parameter δ>0\delta>0, such that for each verifier ii, the result of honest verification is a random variable xix_{i} s.t. P⁡(d⁡(xi,x)<δ)>1−ϵ1P(d(x_{i},x)<\delta)>1-\epsilon_{1}, i.e., the result lies within a small ball centered at xx with high probability. On the other hand, if verifier ii does not perform the honest verification, we assume that he can only do some random guess and report a x~i\tilde{x}_{i}, and P⁡(d⁡(x~i,x)<3​δ)<ϵ2P(d(\tilde{x}_{i},x)<3\delta)<\epsilon_{2}, i.e., he only has a small probability to guess a result within a 3-time radius.

-B Algorithm

We let every verifier i∈[n]i\in[n] independently report their verification results as xix_{i}. Then we run the Kruskal algorithm until the edge length exceeds 2​δ2\delta, getting a forest with vertex set [n][n]. For each connected component C⊆[n]C\subseteq[n], we call CC as a cluster in agreement.

For a given quorum-size q>n2q>\frac{n}{2}, we check if there is a cluster in agreement of size at least qq, called as a “proper cluster”. Because q>n2q>\frac{n}{2}, there can be at most one such proper cluster.

If there is one, the system reaches a consensus that this cluster is accepted, and verifiers outside the cluster are rejected. We accept the inferencer if and only if his result is within 2​δ2\delta distance of a verifier in the proper cluster.

If there is no proper cluster, then the system fails to reach a consensus and invokes the zero-knowledge proof stage. If the inferencer or any verifier disputes about the results, the zero-knowledge proof is also invoked.

-C Analysis

In the analysis, we let n=6,q=4,ϵ1=ϵ2=0.01,r=0.8n=6,q=4,\epsilon_{1}=\epsilon_{2}=0.01,r=0.8. In the calculation we only consider the probability that “the consensus is reached in the voting (i.e., there is a proper cluster) and the verifier is accepted”. As we assume that if the consensus is not reached and the zero-knowledge proof is invoked, the system will get the correct judgment, the actual result will be better even without the disputing process.

-C1 Acceptance Rate of Honest Verifiers

We assume that the verifier 11 is honest, then P⁡(d⁡(x1,x)<δ)>1−ϵ1P(d(x_{1},x)<\delta)>1-\epsilon_{1}.

For verifiers 2,3,⋯,n2,3,\cdots,n, each one has a probability rr to be honest, and each honest verifier has a probability at least 1−ϵ11-\epsilon_{1} to report a result in the ball B⁡(x,δ)B(x,\delta). Hence, each of them has a probability at least pi​n=(1−ϵ1)​rp_{in}=(1-\epsilon_{1})r to report a result in B⁡(x,δ)B(x,\delta).

We can see that if verifier 11 and at least q−1q-1 other verifiers’ reports lie in B⁡(x,δ)B(x,\delta), then they are within 2​δ2\delta distance of each other, hence verifier 11 belongs to a proper cluster and is accepted. Now we estimate the probability of this event.

For the n−1n-1 other verifiers, the probability that at least q−1q-1 lie in B⁡(x,δ)B(x,\delta) is at least ∑k=q−1n−1(n−1k)​pi​nk​(1−pi​n)n−1−k\sum_{k=q-1}^{n-1}\binom{n-1}{k}p_{in}^{k}(1-p_{in})^{n-1-k}. Hence, the probability that verifier 11 is accepted is at least

(1−ϵ1)⋅∑k=q−1n−1(n−1k)​pi​nk​(1−pi​n)n−1−k.(1-\epsilon_{1})\cdot\sum_{k=q-1}^{n-1}\binom{n-1}{k}p_{in}^{k}(1-p_{in})^{n-1-k}.

When n=6,q=4,ϵ1=0.01,r=0.8n=6,q=4,\epsilon_{1}=0.01,r=0.8, we compute that the probability is greater than 92.6%92.6\%.

-C2 Acceptance Rate of Dishonest Verifiers

Wlog we assume that the verifier 11 is dishonest, then P⁡(d⁡(x1,x)<3​δ)<1−ϵ2P(d(x_{1},x)<3\delta)<1-\epsilon_{2}.

For verifiers i∈{2,3,⋯,n}i\in\{2,3,\cdots,n\}, we call ii regular if he reports a result in B⁡(x,δ)B(x,\delta), and have already shown that each of them has at least an independent pi​n=(1−ϵ1)​rp_{in}=(1-\epsilon_{1})r probability to be regular.

We notice that if there is no vertex in B⁡(x,3​δ)−B⁡(x,δ)B(x,3\delta)-B(x,\delta), then a cluster can only be either completely in B⁡(x,δ)B(x,\delta), or completely outside B⁡(x,3​δ)B(x,3\delta). Hence, if the dishonest verifier 11 is accepted, at least one of following events happen:

  1. 1.

    Verifier 11 is in a proper cluster in B⁡(x,δ)B(x,\delta).

  2. 2.

    Verifier 11 is in a proper cluster outside B⁡(x,3​δ)B(x,3\delta).

  3. 3.

    There exists at least one vertex in B⁡(x,3​δ)−B⁡(x,δ)B(x,3\delta)-B(x,\delta).

For the first case, we know that d⁡(x1,x)<δ<3​δd(x_{1},x)<\delta<3\delta, and the probability is at most pd​1=ϵ2p_{d1}=\epsilon_{2}.

For the second case, we know that there exist no more than n−qn-q regular verifiers among {2,3,⋯,n}\{2,3,\cdots,n\}. The probability is upper bounded by

pd2=∑k=0n−q(n−1k)​pi​nk​(1−pi​n)n−1−k.\displaystyle p_{d_{2}}=\sum_{k=0}^{n-q}\binom{n-1}{k}p_{in}^{k}(1-p_{in})^{n-1-k}.

For the third case, the probability that v1v_{1} lies in B⁡(x,3​δ)−B⁡(x,δ)B(x,3\delta)-B(x,\delta) is at most ϵ2\epsilon_{2}, and the probability that each vi​(i≥2)v_{i}(i\geq 2) lies in B⁡(x,3​δ)−B⁡(x,δ)B(x,3\delta)-B(x,\delta) is at most ϵ1​r+ϵ2​(1−r)\epsilon_{1}r+\epsilon_{2}(1-r). So the total probability is upper bounded by

pd3=ϵ2+(n−1)​(ϵ1​r+ϵ2​(1−r)).p_{d_{3}}=\epsilon_{2}+(n-1)\left(\epsilon_{1}r+\epsilon_{2}(1-r)\right).

When n=6,q=4,ϵ1=ϵ2=0.01,r=0.8n=6,q=4,\epsilon_{1}=\epsilon_{2}=0.01,r=0.8, we can compute that pd​1=0.01,pd​2<0.065,pd​3=0.06p_{d1}=0.01,p_{d2}<0.065,p_{d3}=0.06, so the probability that a dishonest verifier gets accepted is less than 12.5%12.5\%.
